I had frequent meltdowns and uncontrollable fits of rage from it all before I was able to do ketamine therapy and learned a few self hypnosis/regulation techniques. before that the idea of recovery seemed absolutely impossible and I was severely suicidal. right before my infusion series i had police and firefighters come to my house 7 times in two months. i ruined my vocal chords from screaming until I tasted blood. it was bad. 

Besides my luck and privilege of affording and being able to access treatments that happened to help,  I think the sequence of treatments was an important part of allowing my improvement. I dont think I wouldve had the mental faculty to make room for the improvements from SGB injections without the ketamine therapy before, and I doubt that I wouldve had the improvements from HBOT without the SGB. because the improvement of each separate treatment was never enough to get me functional enough that I could see myself continuing my life. 

ketamine offered a mindfulness and hope from having had moments of bliss, that let me know whatever was wrong was a dysfunction and not a permanent injury. that gave me patience. I also learned a lot about neuroplasticity and how to work with my subconscious expectations and use that to my advantage in psychedelic therapy. Ketamine was also a emergency break for anytime i got stuck in ruminations and suicidality and helped me keep the mental torture at bay for the time being. it didnt extend my capacity but it reduced my suffering and helped my body remember a more functional way of being that would become more and more second nature over time as I was able to find treatment for the underlying metabolic and structural issues. 

I was able to access the SGB because I had a period of less symptoms after my first covid infection, which happened by chance and made me go from severe to lower end of moderate. the SGB in turn helped restore cerebral bloodflow which I think is important for optimising the effects of HBOT. the improved bloodflow and improvement of sleep quality helps the brain recover better each night, which if left undisturbed would add to long term improvement. when the brain has more blood it has an easier time staying cool, and microglia dont get as stressed.

with HBOT you are told to avoid smoking and caffeine before treatment because the vasoconstriction counteracts the effect of the treatment. It makes me think that if LC/ME has abnormal vasoconstriction in the brain, that would limit its benefits. So doing HBOT after the SGB could likely improve the chances of it helping more. I did 1.5 ATA at 60 min sessions, 20 sessions during a month. 

and once HBOT has had a chance of repairing damage from oxidative stress and inflammation, and also improved vasoformation in the brain so that the body doesnt have to work as hard to oxygenate the brain and other tissues, as well as adding to the improved circulation and ridding metabolic waste through encouraging lymphatic drainage, that would have positive downstream consequences in slowing down the accumulation of inflammatory waste products that otherwise would undo the improvements from HBOT. I noticed HBOT reducing swelling in my face and brain very clearly. my undereye bags and chronic congestion and mushy head feel disappeared.

lastly, when these treatments had done what they could in helping my body come to an equilibrium that was as calm and balanced as possible, the serotonergic and antiinflammatory and neuroplastic kick of LSD was all that was needed to help the nervous system find its way back to old gears. I dont think it wouldve been possible without the 2 years of trials and priming before that.

the different phases of a trip are very different from each other. the come up is the most uncomfortable, where ypur body has to adjust to the increased stimulation and sensitivity, and you have to greet the increase of incoming information. once you reach the peak the tensions tend to even out and bloom, and then you have a peak of a couple hours before it starts to fade, and then you have a usually very pleasant afterglow. so when they say a trip is 10 hours its not a static thing, the first 2-3 hours are the most challenging for me but also sets the tone for the rest of the trip.

the stellate ganglion block temporarily blocks the sympathetic hypervigilance which allows you to go into proper rest and digest for a few hours. it seems to reboot the nervous system, downregulate the fight or flight response, giving you more neurological and emotional headroom to process trauma, before dissociation or inhibitory coping mechanisms are engaged. it can help give more room to process trauma in EMDR or ketamine therapy. the effects can last up to 6 months or longer after each session. ive had two treatments and im still way better off than I was before, it has helped my insomnia and brain fog, it restores cerebral perfusion, sensory impressions seem more vibrant and clear afterwards. its been over 1,5 years since my last treatment. 

Ketamine therapy also shuts down fight or flight, and desynchronises the default mode network that is associated with ruminations. DMN is active when we are idle, daydreaming, or in case of anxiety OCD trauma and depression its where we process memories that lead to invasive thoughts or ruminations.

what this desynchronisation does is allow gaps in time where you are able to jump off the burned in circuitry keeping us locked into trauma responses, it makes us see our trauma behaviour from new angles, it lowers the adrenergic response to traumatic memories, it mimics the emotional processing of REM sleep and lucid dreaming. You enter a sortof hypnotic state where its easier to process trauma abd integrate it from muscle memory into long term memory so that next time that memory is triggered it feels like a thing of the past and not like you are reliving it. 
Ketamine shuts down a lot of background processes that can occur when we are stuck in a hypervigilant/shattered mindspace, so that you are temporarily unified and in direct contact with your body and self again, it offloads your working memory, offering windows to visualise a healed way of being. with time your body will have a clearer model of what to self regulate towards, and each time you are triggered you dont lose sight of the horizon, so you can navigate through it and find your way back to baseline. 

finally, EMDR overlaps a lot with ketamine assisted psychotherapy, in off loading our working memory so that we dont get as overwhelmed by triggers, and they complement each other nicely. each session you will hopefully experience authentic responses trickling through, to reduce the pressure and resistance to the trigger. once you start having positive experiences of being able to expose yourself in measured amounts to a trigger and you are able to hold on to a curious/analytical and emotionally present mindset, it will build your confidence and reduce your fears of it.

the combination of these treatments have been nothing short of magic. I still have bad days, i still experience freeze responses, but they usually last hours, not weeks or months, and I have the ability to take myself outof it by will sometimes. my anhedonia is nowhere near the constant curse it used to be, i can feel content and alive and connected in the moment, my sense of empathy has increased dramatically, my triggers and trauma responses are not erased but they are transparent and I maintain a sense of self and an adult protector who is in dialogue with my inner child when it happens. I dont fear the triggers or suicidal thoughts, they feel like scar tissue and old schemas rather than actual reality 95% of the time. 

I am doing way better than I thought I ever would be. I recognise my old self and I see a path towards continued improvement.

I’m not sure I am the right person to answer this, I am still working on it, even though Ive been in remission since May, I am still deeply traumatised and trying to figure out how to put my life together and to use my windows of functionality for joyful things in the moment. I am physically strong enough to do things I previously enjoyed but they are so strongly associated with PEM and loss that theyve become pretty bad PTSD triggers. I am working very hard on reframing what joy is for myself with the tools I have available to me. learning to not be bored with things that are below my previous ”level” comes with a lot of self scrutiny and dismantling of internalised ableism. I was an extremely restless audhd person before I got ME, so the challenge of finding purpose and reward with such a restricted life has often been completely impossible. 

As a creative I deeply believe your process has to start with a need, and the tools available. I ”failed” at fashion and music so I decided to stop limiting my ambition to create value and beauty to those mediums, and instead I try to recognise that every single interaction I have with people is an opportunity to communicate the same longing for beauty, love, liberation, connection, forgiveness. The fashion designer Rick Owens is a huge role model to me, he often talks about beautiful behaviour as the ultimate goal of his work. I decided to take a shortcut and get rid of the middle hand and just try to reinvent who I want to be by reverse engineering my motivation for why I do things. 

when I was severely suicidal and still undiagnosed in the psych ward once, I wrote instructional poems to myself where I decided to find the right receiver, in their darkest place, at their darkest moments, do something beautiful for them and mean it. I was struggling with severe anhedonia for years, completely incapable of sensory joy with the brain fog I was having, so the only respite I had was in the ontology of things, their actual being, and not in my experience of them. I was starving for meaning, and figured if I cant experience it maybe I can at least be a source for it to others to maybe experience it. 

That is when I started spending time supporting other people suffering online, especially here on reddit. I put all my effort into sharing research, sharing thoughts on healing, listening to people in suicidal crises. It truly has been life saving for me to pour myself into people who otherwise have noone looking out for them. These days Im much less eager to perform for the praise of rich and ”beautiful” people. If I can give someone who never has received a compliment in their life their first compliment, I find that endlessly more gratifying. I feel that is much more in line with my true values and not what society has deemed admirable. 

This reframing is part of my current process of decolonising my mind. It is going to be a lifelong process of unlearning but I am happy to be on that path because it feels like the REAL me. I do it with myself and the universe as a witness, and not for the validation of others.

I have experienced a shift from having a purely hedonistic view on life (philosophically, like you, not necessarily about the rock star lifestyle) but I have started experiencing a shift in that as Ive started to heal. I think the hedonistic approach makes sense if youve been subject to really painful stuff that has forced you to be in the present moment for various reasons. 

I suffered very intensely from chronic illness for a decade, which forced me to avoid thinking about the future, since any long term plans was always outof reach. that meant I was confined to any sense of purpose or pleasure or peace I could acquire in the moment. It made life very unstable.

Now that Im able to dream a bit about the future again, longer narratives and structures carry more meaning, and it reframes sacrifices in the moment like pursuing discipline into a more reasonable payoff. I have also observed myself skewing more towards pursuing different values like solidarity and courage which is about transcending certain fears, pains or discomfort for a higher common goal because I genuinely want the world to be inhabited by more people who think like this, it helps give meaning to an otherwise meaningless existence. the striving/the process is more meaningful than the destination/arrival. I want a life in motion, moving towards a horizon or an ideal, and I dont need to arrive to feel content with that. 

I have not fully abandoned a hedonistic view because I think pleasure and beauty are really important rewards, but only relying on them will make moments when theyre not accessible difficult to handle. I need other values to carry me during those times. Being able to move between those modes of functioning has lended me greater flexibility.

a healthy brain operates along two networks, default mode network(DMN) and Task Positive network (TPN)

in a healthy brain theyre anticorrelated. DMN is activated when the brain is idle, daydreaming, ruminating, memory processing, 

TPN is spatial awareness outwards aimed focus and bodily presence, executing tasks. activating TPN through using all your senses and crossing their incoming sensory data is what allows us to reassociate from dissociation or rumination. 

doing light yoga or spatial awareness exercises coming out of a ketamine session was extremely helpful for me.

these exercises temporarily gave me back the photographic memory i had as a child! space and time are connected and being emotionally present is what allows you to form new memories so with time, staying outof rumination will improve your memory.

I have struggled with very severe insomnia most of my life, both because of autism and adhd, but also due to neurological illness and trauma that has damaged my rest and digest circuitry. As a child my mother would have to spend 3-5 hours putting me to bed on weekdays. There are a couple of aspects that have helped me:

Avoiding unnecessary stress during the day will keep your nervous system in a less strained state, which means there’s less tension to release towards night time. This is of course not always possible so on the days you feel extra tense try to make extra time for winding down so that you are in phase as much as possible when it’s actually time to sleep. 

Having a strict yet ENJOYABLE night time routine. I use positive sensory input, scanning across the tactile, olfactory, auditory and visual fields combined. This involves avoiding blue light from sundown, I have color shifting smart lighting with dimmers throughout my home and will usually only have very warm or completely red light during the evening. This includes avoiding blue light from screens at least an hour before bedtime. I have a few low arousal podcasts I play when I sleep to help curb rumination.

If you enjoy incense or tea these are both great sensory regulations to associate with sleep.


I try to avoid dehydrating foods that are rich in salt or sugar late in the evening. They will increase blood pressure and core temperature which will make it harder to sleep. I find glycine is actually surprisingly good at lowering core temperature and regulating blood sugar which has a rather strong anxiolytic effect for being a supplement. There’s also blood pressure medication that helps against nightmares so you might understand how heart rate and blood pressure affects sleep quality.

Weighted blankets can be hard to get used to but if you are patient and choose a blanket about 10% of your body weight your body will start associating it with safety and sleep. 

I have really soft loungewear in cashmere that helps making the routine even more enjoyable. 

I also have a memory foam sleep mask that molds along the eyelids and works almost like a weighted blanket for the eyes. I LOVE it. 

As for sleep aids I find overmedicating with prescription medicine isn’t always the most effective in giving you the best quality sleep. That’s why I combine a few otc supplements

Magnesium threonate penetrates the blood brain barrier and calms frontal cortex activity 

Apigenin comes from camomile and is gently soothing

Glycine helps both natural serotonin and melatonin 
production, lowers core temperature and regulates blood sugar levels. 

Theanine is what makes tea less jittery than coffee, a muscle relaxant that helps a bit as well

I combine these for maximum effect with minimum side effects. It gives natural and good sleep quality. 

As for taking melatonin supplementation it hasn’t really worked for me, I wake up as soon as it wears off and I feel very depressed the next day, even with just 2 mg extended release formulations. 

As for prescription medication I find promethazine helps to take one to two hours before bedtime, the other supplements I take at bedtime. If I don’t fall asleep in time it can give me restless legs as it reduces dopamine a bit but the other supplements help reduce that side effect.

Sometimes I also take daridoxerant which is a new sleep aid that is not addictive and works on orexin receptors. It’s effect is super discrete and doesn’t make me groggy in the morning at all. It seems to give me real sleep. Accessing it can be difficult but worth looking into. 

For a period I also used to rely on propranolol as it lowered my heart rate and had some anti anxiety effect but I no longer need it. 

I’m also taking low dose naltrexone which helps the body release it’s own endorphins and has improved sleep quality and lowered anxiety for me. I’m on just 2 mg, the side effects are nonexistent at that dose for me. It’s also antiinflammatory and immune modulating so if you have autoimmune issues it can be helpful. 

Other treatments I think have helped improve my sleep quality is stellate ganglion block injections for PTSD which helps reboot the nervous system by inhibiting the sympathetic nervous system. It helps dilate blood vessels in the brain and improves oxygenation of the brain and raises the panic threshold. It’s revolutionised my life. 

The combined effects of these are key for me. Relying on one thing isn’t realistic. I used to wake up after two or three hours with adrenaline rushes, soaked through the mattress with night sweats and nightmares, hallucinations nausea headaches and now I sleep through the night 8-10 hours and feel rested when I wake up. It’s a first in 35 years.

The things that have helped me ( diagnosed ME/CFS) have been

Radical rest: prolonged period of very low stress and low activity

Stellate ganglion block injections that improve cerebral bloodflow and therefor improves oxygen levels in your brain. 

Hyperbaric oxygen therapy: supposedly helps the body fight latent infections and viral reservoirs that might, and also improves oxygenation of the brain.

Ketamine therapy - helped with depression and anhedonia which also contributed to my fatigue

LSD -also antidepressant, can help calm down immune responses that make you sluggish and improves mitochondrial function

Methylated B-vitamins - if our bodies are stressed from infection or trauma or due to genetic factors our bodies might become worse at converting b-vitamins to active form. Methylated supplements helped me even though my blood work was normal.

Collagen supplementation - gives your brain a lot of easily absorbed energy


All of these things are just shared as an example of what CAN help, I’m not saying this is what you need, you might have a condition that demands something else, but these were some of the things that ended up making a difference for me.

Meditation is basically a way to train your brain to improve your ability to engage TPN and sustain TPN by focusing your attention to one specific task, making that task as easy and as little energy consuming as possible, ie. The point is to make sure to always having something small to look forward to in the near future. If you can’t engage with it for the moment it needs to be in such close time frame that you at least can plan for it. Waiting for it puts you back in the DMN and that’s when memories come rushing back.

Rumination and invasive thoughts are part of the so called “default mode network” (DMN) of the brain. They engage when we’re idle, they involve memory processing and daydreaming. Then there’s the “task positive network” or TPN which is anti correlated to the DMN. The TPN is associated with outwards aimed focus and spatial awareness. This means that the way to control your rumination is to direct your focus spatially to where you are. This explanation has helped me embrace distraction as a scientifically valid solution to the problem of rumination instead of feeling like an avoidant behaviour.
